papers.title: Population-scale immunoglobulin genomics links inherited variation to antibody repertoire organization
papers.authors: Peres, A.; Jana, U.; Rodriguez, O.; Vanwinkle, Z. M.; Engelbrecht, E.; Gibson, W. S.; Shields, K.; Croslin, B.; Schultze, S.; Bharadwaj, C.; Murray, C.; Lees, W. D.; Smith, M. L.; Watson, C. T.; Yaari, G.
papers.abstract: Human antibody repertoires emerge from inherited immunoglobulin variation interacting with V(D)J recombination and selection, yet how population-level germline diversity contributes to repertoire organization remains incompletely understood. We integrated long-read genomic data across the IGH, IGK, and IGL loci from 871 individuals, including 172 individuals with matched antibody repertoire sequencing. We identify extensive previously unrepresented genetic diversity and show that coding variation is embedded within a smaller set of recurrent RSS and leader sequence architectures. Integrating genomic and repertoire data further reveals genotype-associated differences in conditional segment usage that are not captured by conventional gene-usage analysis, and an association between IGK genotype similarity and exact CDR3 amino acid sharing across individuals. Together, these results reveal multiple levels at which inherited immunoglobulin variation is associated with the organization of expressed antibody repertoires. The underlying sequences and genomic and repertoire evidence are provided through the Human Unified Set of Alleles (HUSA), enabling genotype-aware analysis of immunoglobulin variation across diverse human populations.

papers.title: Structural clustering of paired αβ T-cell receptor repertoires recovers antigen-specific convergence beyond sequence similarity
papers.authors: Srai, D.; Aarts, D.; Frater, J.; Raybould, M.
papers.abstract: T-cell receptor (TCR) antigen recognition depends on the three-dimensional geometry of the paired {beta} complementarity-determining regions (CDRs), which primary sequence does not fully capture. Most repertoire-clustering methods group receptors by CDR3 motifs, sequence distance or V-J gene usage, and may miss receptors that differ in sequence but adopt similar loop conformations. We present SPACE-TCR (Structural Profiling of Alpha-Beta Clonotypes by Epitope), which stratifies predicted paired {beta} backbone models by CDR length, aligns them on conserved framework anchors and clusters them by C RMSD across the CDRs. On an independently curated benchmark of 4,779 paired CD8 TCRs spanning 367 epitopes, 94.6% of SPACE-TCR clusters at the focal 0.75 [A] threshold had purity [≥] 0.9, close to ClusTCR (97.3%), while clustering more than twice as many unique CDR3{beta} (10.4% versus 4.7%); every method that clustered more did so at markedly lower purity. SPACE-TCR had the lowest polyspecificity (5.4%), and 22.7% of its high-purity clusters were sequence-diverse or sequence-unrelated, categories rarely recovered by the evaluated CDR3{beta}-similarity methods. With increasing unannotated repertoire background, it kept higher purity than the evaluated sequence-based methods across all available comparisons (30.4% at 89.2% noise, compared with 15.0% for TCRMatch). Paired structural clustering therefore complements sequence-based analysis, recovering convergent receptor families that sequence criteria miss.

papers.title: Obesity-associated changes in immune cell dynamics during alphavirus infection revealed by single-cell transcriptomic analysis.
papers.authors: Hameed M, Rai P, Daamen AR, Tiller K, Hossain MS, Carvallo FR, Coutermarsh-Ott S, Lipsky PE, Weger-Lucarelli J.
papers.abstract: Obesity alters host immunity, resulting in worse disease outcomes following infection with various pathogens, including arthritogenic alphaviruses. However, the impact of obesity on the functional landscape of immune cells during acute arthritogenic alphavirus infection remains incompletely explored. Here, we used single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) to dissect the blood and tissue immune responses to Mayaro virus (MAYV) infection in lean and obese mice. Footpad injection of MAYV caused significant shifts in immune cell populations and induced robust expression of interferon response and proinflammatory cytokine genes and related pathways in both blood and tissue. In MAYV-infected lean mice, single-cell analysis of the footpad response revealed a unique macrophage subset (F4/80 lo MHCII + ) with high expression of interferon-responsive genes that was replaced by an alternative, F4/80 int population in infected obese mice. Macrophages isolated from lean mice had higher levels of inflammatory gene expression. Furthermore, obese macrophages infected with MAYV and CHIKV ex vivo produce an immunoregulatory response (IL-10) compared to lean macrophages that produce a higher pro-inflammatory response (TNF). The stronger inflammatory response in lean macrophages was associated with less severe systemic disease in lean mice. These results provide evidence for the role of a unique population of macrophages that may contribute to the superior capacity of lean mice to control arthritogenic alphavirus infection.IMPORTANCEArthritogenic alphaviruses-including chikungunya, Mayaro, and Ross River viruses-cause chronic, often disabling joint and muscle disease and are expanding into new regions, yet no approved therapies target the disease process itself. Obesity is a known risk factor for more severe outcomes after infection, but the underlying immune mechanisms have been unclear. Using single-cell RNA sequencing, we show that infection drives widespread interferon and inflammatory responses in blood and infected tissue and that obesity specifically alters the macrophage populations present at the infection site. Lean mice mount a highly activated, interferon-driven macrophage response linked to better control of local inflammation, while obese mice instead accumulate a related but less activated population enriched for necroptosis-associated genes and linked to greater tissue damage. These findings identify a specific macrophage subset as a likely contributor to the more severe alphavirus disease seen with obesity and a potential target for future therapies.

papers.title: Nuciferine Inhibits Gastric Cancer Progression and Potentiates Immunotherapy by Targeting HSP90α.
papers.authors: Liu W, Yang Z, Dong H, Wang B, Tang H, Ma H, Li Y, Li F, Liu Y, Tan B.
papers.abstract: Nuciferine exhibits potential anticancer properties, but its role and mechanisms in Gastric cancer (GC) remain unclear. Multi-database collection of nuciferine-related target genes, WGCNA analysis of GC differential gene sets, and Cytoscape, STRING, and MCODE network analyses identified key genes. Molecular docking and SPR were employed to determine critical target genes. Survival analysis, KEGG network analysis, immune infiltration analysis, ROC curve analysis, and single-cell analysis were conducted to explore potential mechanisms. Clinical data were collected for pathological correlation analysis. We conducted gene overexpression, CCK-8 assay, scratch healing assay, transwell assay, colony formation assay, immunohistochemical staining, co-culture of cells, flow cytometry, RT-qPCR, western blot, and in vivo experiments to verify the role of nuciferine in GC. Among the candidate targets, HSP90AA1 showed the strongest correlation with nuciferine and exhibited a strong molecular interaction. HSP90AA1 was positively correlated with the suppressive immune microenvironment of gastric cancer and poorer patient prognosis, and was associated with TNM staging, vascular tumor thrombus, PD-L1-CPS scores, CD117 + mast cell infiltration, and CD8 + T cell infiltration in GC patients. Nuciferine inhibits the proliferation, migration, and invasion abilities of GC cells, reduces the expression levels of P-AKT and P-mTOR, and can suppress the growth of tumors in mice. Overexpression of HSP90AA1 rescued nuciferine's effects. Co-culture experiments demonstrated that nuciferine inhibited the increase in the number of IL-10 + , TGF-β + , and PD-L1 + mast cells induced by GC cells. Meanwhile, nuciferine decreased the expression levels of IL-2 and IL-6 and increased the expression levels of CCL3 and TNF-α in mast cells. In vivo experiments have confirmed that the combination of nuciferine and PD-1 inhibitors has a promoting effect. This study elucidates the mechanism by which nuciferine targets HSP90α to inhibit GC progression and enhance immunotherapy efficacy, positioning nuciferine as a promising adjuvant and therapeutic strategy for GC.

papers.title: Ferroptosis-related molecular signatures in Alzheimer's disease and the neuroprotective effects of allicin: an integrated bioinformatics, peripheral single-cell transcriptomic, and experimental study.
papers.authors: Wang B, Feng ZZ, Zhang M, Wang Y.
papers.abstract: Ferroptosis is increasingly implicated in Alzheimer's disease (AD), but the relationship between AD-associated transcriptomic changes, peripheral immune alterations, and candidate ferroptosis-modulating compounds remains incompletely defined. This study aimed to identify ferroptosis-related molecular signatures associated with AD and to evaluate whether allicin attenuates ferroptosis-related injury in complementary experimental models. Human hippocampal microarray datasets GSE1297 and GSE28146 were examined with explicit consideration of donor overlap; GSE1297 was treated as the primary subject-level reference dataset, whereas the donor-overlapping GSE28146 dataset was used only as a cross-platform sensitivity source and not as an independent cohort. Ferroptosis-related candidates were prioritized using FerrDb, AD-related annotation, protein-protein interaction analysis, and pathway analysis. Peripheral-blood single-cell RNA-sequencing data (GSE181279) were analyzed to describe immune-cell composition and peripheral distribution of candidate genes without extrapolating these findings to brain-parenchymal cell localization. Candidate-drug prediction and molecular docking were followed by D-galactose/AlCl3 rat experiments and erastin-treated PC12-cell experiments. Histology, ROS, Western blotting, RT-qPCR, and JC-1 assays were used to assess ferroptosis-related molecular and mitochondrial changes. Ferroptosis-focused transcriptomic screening and network prioritization highlighted GPX4, FSP1, SLC7A11, TFRC, and ACSL4 as candidate genes for subsequent analyses. Their expression pattern was compatible with reduced antioxidant defense and increased iron/lipid-peroxidation susceptibility in AD-associated hippocampal transcriptomes. Peripheral single-cell analysis showed heterogeneous expression of these genes across T-cell, B-cell, NK-cell, monocyte, and platelet populations; these results are interpreted as peripheral immune context rather than evidence of brain-cell localization. Molecular docking predicted energetically favorable allicin-protein poses, but does not establish direct target engagement. In the experimental models, allicin attenuated histopathological injury and ROS accumulation, shifted GPX4, FSP1, SLC7A11, TFRC, and ACSL4 expression in an anti-ferroptotic direction, and improved mitochondrial membrane-potential readouts, with changes directionally similar to ferrostatin-1. The combined data support an association between AD-related molecular changes and ferroptosis-regulatory pathways and show that allicin can reduce ferroptosis-related injury in the models used. Because the human datasets include donor overlap, the single-cell dataset is peripheral rather than brain-derived, and direct target-engagement, lipidomic, genetic-rescue, and pharmacokinetic experiments were not performed, the findings should be considered mechanistically suggestive rather than proof that allicin directly targets the five proteins or specifically inhibits AD-associated ferroptosis in humans.

papers.title: Locoregional administration of bispecific CAR-T cells targeting CD44 and CD133 in recurrent high-grade glioma: a first-in-human investigator-initiated trial.
papers.authors: Zhai Y, Li G, Wang A, Kahlert UD, Xu Q, Xu M, Xia X, Qian Z, Jiang T, Zhang W.
papers.abstract: Grade IV glioma remains highly lethal, and effective therapies for recurrent disease remain limited. Glioma stem cells (GSCs) contribute to therapeutic resistance and tumor recurrence, providing a rationale for GSC-targeted immunotherapy. We conducted a single-center, single-arm investigator-initiated trial evaluating locoregional administration of CD44/CD133 bispecific chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells incorporating a truncated interleukin-7 receptor α (IL-7Rα) intracellular domain in ten adults with recurrent grade IV glioma. Treatment was well tolerated, with no dose-limiting toxicities or Grade ≥2 cytokine release syndrome. Adverse events were predominantly mild and transient, and no patient required IL-6 or IL-1 blockade. CAR-T cell leakage into peripheral blood remained minimal, whereas cerebrospinal fluid cytokine elevations were modest following infusion. Three patients achieved partial responses. The median overall survival after the first CAR-T cell infusion was 465 days. Exploratory single-cell RNA sequencing and proteomic analyses suggested patient stratification in macrophage-associated signatures, particularly in interferon signaling and antigen-presentation programs, which were associated with distinct clinical outcomes independently of IDH mutation status in this cohort. These findings demonstrate the feasibility and safety of repeated locoregional administration of GSC-targeting IL-7Rα-armored bispecific CAR-T cells. Exploratory immune profiling further identified inter-patient heterogeneity in macrophage-associated immune programs, which warrants validation in larger prospective studies. (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05577091, NMPA No. CXSL2500032).

papers.title: A disulfidptosis related five-lncRNA signature for prognosis stratification and immune microenvironment characterization in clear cell renal cell carcinoma.
papers.authors: Zhou B, Tang R, Jiang L, Miao P, Wan Y, Yu S, Li G, Liao T, Ma W, Dai R.
papers.abstract: BackgroundClear cell renal cell carcinoma is an aggressive disease associated with poor outcomes. Disulfidptosis is a recently identified form of cell death triggered by disulfide stress in actin cytoskeletal proteins. This study aimed to construct a prognostic model using disulfidptosis-related lncRNAs in clear cell renal cell carcinoma.MethodsThis retrospective bioinformatics study analyzed The Cancer Genome Atlas clear cell renal cell carcinoma data to identify disulfidptosis-related lncRNAs and construct a prognostic risk model using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator and Cox regression, followed by nomogram development and evaluation of immune infiltration. To further characterize the biological relevance of the model, preliminary in vitro experiments were conducted to validate the expression and functional effects of the identified lncRNAs, and single-cell RNA sequencing data from GSE152938 were used to explore risk score-associated tumor-cell heterogeneity and intercellular communication.ResultsA five-lncRNA prognostic model comprising AC084024.4, LINC01522, AC091563.1, SPINT1-AS1, and LINC01963 was constructed and showed robust predictive performance in the Cancer Genome Atlas training, testing, and entire cohorts. Reverse transcription quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction confirmed their differential expression in tumor tissues, and functional experiments demonstrated differential effects on the migration and invasion of OSRC2 cells. Single-cell analysis of GSE152938 further identified distinct tumor-cell states associated with the prognostic signature, with tumor cells in the high-risk state showing stronger intercellular communication and enhanced chemotaxis-related signaling, accompanied by alterations in genes related to the cytoskeleton and metabolism.ConclusionDisulfidptosis-related lncRNAs may represent potential prognostic biomarkers for clear cell renal cell carcinoma. We established a five-lncRNA signature with prognostic relevance and experimental support, and single-cell analysis suggested that risk-associated tumor-cell states were linked to altered tumor-immune communication and chemotaxis-related signaling. These findings provide new insights into the biological relevance of disulfidptosis-related lncRNAs in clear cell renal cell carcinoma, although independent validation and mechanistic studies remain necessary for future clinical translation.

papers.title: Hibernation-Driven Immune Suppression in Thirteen-Lined Ground Squirrels
papers.authors: Zhao, M.; Chen, J.; Burrett, R.; Yang, W.; Mandal, S.; Lohani, S. C.; Zhang, C.; Wickramasinghe, J.; Andrews, M. T.; Li, Q.
papers.abstract: Torpor in mammals imposes extreme energetic constraints, yet how it reshapes the immune system remains poorly understood. Here we characterized splenic immune remodeling during torpor relative to the pre-hibernation active state in a natural hibernator, the 13-lined ground squirrel, using single-cell RNA sequencing, immunohistochemical staining, and quantitative image analysis. The torpid spleen showed a significantly reduced white-pulp area fraction with a preferential reduction of B cell- and T cell-rich adaptive niches and relative preservation of innate myeloid populations. Among splenic immune cells, the relative frequency of B cells was significantly lower and that of macrophages significantly higher in torpid animals. Across five immune cell types examined (B cells, T cells, macrophages, dendritic cells, and neutrophils), torpid animals exhibited more than 2-fold higher Cirbp expression (nominal P < 0.05); Txnip was also higher and Hk2 lower, with adjusted P < 0.05 in B and T cells, suggesting reduced glycolysis in these cells. In B and T cells, canonical pathway analysis predicted inhibition of mitogen-activated protein kinase, mTOR, and chemokine signaling, together with activation of capped intron-containing pre-mRNA processing. In myeloid cells, predicted pathway changes differed by cell type, including inhibition of the RHO GTPase cycle in macrophages and of inflammasome signaling in dendritic cells, and activation of interleukin-1 family signaling in neutrophils. These findings identify selective splenic immune remodeling associated with torpor, characterized by a reduced white-pulp area fraction and altered immune cell composition, accompanied by shared changes in Cirbp, Txnip, and Hk2 expression and cell-type-specific transcriptional responses.

papers.title: Selective suppression and biasing of chemokine receptors CCR9 and ACKR4 through targeting CCL25 with de novo miniproteins.
papers.authors: de Boer B, Lamme TD, Verdwaald K, Santamaria Medina S, Németh CG, Elfrink EM, Smit M, de Esch IJP, Schafer CT.
papers.abstract: Chemokines and their receptors mediate cell migration and coordinate immune responses, while dysregulation can lead to inflammation. Therapeutic modulation of the chemokine signaling axis has proven difficult. Most drug discovery efforts target the receptors, whereas natural regulatory mechanisms modulate immune responses by directly binding to or modifying the chemokine ligands. Despite this insight, development of effective chemokine-directed modulators has remained elusive. Recent advances in de novo protein design offer an unprecedented opportunity to produce high-affinity binders that efficiently block protein-protein interactions. We implemented a computational workflow leveraging the BindCraft platform to generate miniprotein binders against CCL25, the chemokine ligand for the receptors CCR9 and ACKR4, and implicated in inflammatory bowel diseases. The unbiased development results in several miniproteins designed to block the receptor N-terminus from wrapping the chemokine and preventing productive engagement. Thus, these proteins suppress CCL25-mediated effector coupling and halt MOLT-4 lymphoblast migration. Another class of miniprotein, represented by VUP25111, is predicted to bind CCL25 along the chemokine β1 strand and retained receptor binding. This complex inhibited arrestin recruitment to CCR9, but not to ACKR4, indicating receptor specificity. Additionally, G protein recruitment to CCR9 was unimpeded by VUP25111, suggesting that the miniprotein biased the native agonist towards G proteins. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of differentially targeting CCL25 to suppress CCR9 signaling and new tools to resolve the structural basis of chemokine receptor activation and bias.

papers.title: Multiomics pan‑cancer analysis identifies CA9 as an immunosuppression‑linked prognostic biomarker: Validation of oncogenic and radiomic‑based predictive value in hepatocellular carcinoma.
papers.authors: Zhang Y, Liu J, Wang Z, Wu S, Liang R.
papers.abstract: Carbonic anhydrase IX (CA9) is a tumor-associated transmembrane metalloenzyme implicated in tumor progression, yet its pan-cancer roles and biomarker potential remain underexplored. In this study, we performed the comprehensive and systematic pan-cancer multi-omics analysis of CA9 using data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and multiple analytical platforms, and further validated its functional significance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) through cellular experiments. A radiomics model was also constructed from CT imaging data to predict CA9 expression and prognosis in HCC. Our results showed that CA9 mRNA was significantly upregulated in most cancers and associated with poor prognosis. High CA9 expression correlated with tumor mutation burden, microsatellite instability, tumor heterogeneity, immune cell infiltration, and immune checkpoint molecules. Single-cell data revealed predominant CA9 expression in malignant cells, and pathway enrichment suggested an association between CA9 expression and HIF-1, PI3K-Akt-mTOR signaling, and efferocytosis pathways. Functional experiments confirmed that CA9 promotes HCC cell proliferation, migration, and invasion. Collectively, CA9 shows potential as a pan-cancer diagnostic and prognostic biomarker and is associated with immune-related features, with a possible role in HCC progression. The radiomics model offers a non-invasive approach for predicting CA9 expression.

papers.title: Longitudinal mapping reveals stromal-immune mechanisms underlying reversal of bone marrow fibrosis in myelofibrosis.
papers.authors: Benabid A, Grasshoff M, Pearce JE, Klöker V, Flosdorf N, Rösch L, Reimer KC, Götz K, Wanner P, Lutterbach N, Schalla C, Wanek P, Schmidt L, Ruiz Tejada Segura M, Saad M, Joodaki M, Nagai J, Palm L, Schmitz S, Fuchs SNR, Greven L, Bräsen JH, Schmitz J, Begemann M, Kurth I, Hayat S, Bruch PM, Dietrich S, Bilbao A, Medyouf H, Hofmann UK, Kühnel MP, Boor P, Ackermann M, Jonigk D, Hölzel M, Bindels E, Schäfersküpper M, Ayuk F, Kröger N, Heidel FH, Koschmieder S, Brümmendorf TH, Kramann R, Schneider C, Gleitz HFE, Crysandt M, Costa IG, Schneider RK.
papers.abstract: Myelofibrosis (MF) is characterized by progressive bone marrow (BM) fibrosis that can regress following allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT). To investigate how the human BM microenvironment is remodeled in this unique setting of fibrosis reversal, we generated a longitudinal single-cell atlas of 29 BM biopsies before and after allo-HSCT. Adipogenic CXCL12-abundant reticular (Adipo-CAR) cells were the predominant fibrosis-associated stromal population, with inflammatory reprogramming involving SPP1 + macrophages. Allo-HSCT reversed TGF-β-associated Adipo-CAR-megakaryocyte crosstalk before histological fibrosis regression. Fibrotic cellular neighborhoods were dismantled early, preceding extracellular matrix remodeling, alongside restoration of hematopoietic and immune homeostasis. Across JAK2- and CALR-mutant disease, shared interactions between malignant hematopoietic progenitors, SPP1 + macrophages and Adipo-CARs converged on identifying CD93 as a mediator of mutant-stromal crosstalk. Expression of phosphodiesterase-5A (PDE5A) marked fibrotic stromal activation, and genetic or pharmacological targeting of PDE5A attenuated fibrosis in experimental models. Together, these findings define mechanisms of human fibrosis reversal and reveal actionable targets for non-transplant antifibrotic therapies.

papers.title: Fractal transport barriers govern immune-cell infiltration into heterogeneous solid tumors.
papers.authors: Abolfath RM.
papers.abstract: The therapeutic activity of cytotoxic lymphocytes requires transport from perfused vessels through a geometrically disordered tumor microenvironment before target-cell contact. Standard diffusion models replace this environment by a homogeneous Euclidean continuum and therefore cannot separate restricted accessible volume from scale-dependent motility. Here a multiscale physical model is developed in which the accessible stromal measure has Hausdorff dimension D f , the effective random-motility coefficient decreases with inward depth as a power law governed by a tortuosity exponent θ, and chemotactic persistence and cell loss enter through dimensionless Péclet and Damköhler numbers. A conservative finite-volume solution is paired with biased random walks on site-percolation clusters. The continuum calculations predict boundary accumulation together with severe depletion of the deep tail: at 360 min, increasing disorder from (D f , θ) = (3, 0) to (2.4, 0.6) reduces the mean depth of infiltrating cells from 215 to 125 µm and the normalized density at 500 µm by more than two orders of magnitude. The lattice model identifies a complementary connectivity transition. At 4000 attempted steps, reducing the open-site fraction from p = 0.85 to p = 0.60 lowers the fraction of all injected cells reaching the distal half from 0.782 to 0.007. These results distinguish three experimentally measurable barriers-vascular entry, fractal interstitial transport, and target encounter-and show why a large perivascular immune-cell count need not imply effective tumor-core surveillance. The framework yields falsifiable relations among segmented matrix geometry, single-cell trajectories, and spatial immune-density profiles, and provides compact computational models for calibration to tumor-slice or intravital-imaging data.

papers.title: A preexisting MT-ND3-linked OXPHOS-dominant monocyte state constrains vaccine responsiveness in immunocompromised patients.
papers.authors: Peng ZY, Chen CH, Lin CL, Liao HT, Wang JR, Ko TM.
papers.abstract: Vaccine failure remains common in immunocompromised populations, yet the baseline immune states from host factors that precede poor responsiveness are poorly understood. To address this clinical bottleneck, we investigated whether vaccine nonresponsiveness is already encoded before antigen exposure by using high-dimensional, subset-resolved single-cell analysis in a longitudinal kidney transplant recipient cohort. With 438,088 immune cell profiles, we identified a pre-vaccination monocyte NR program marked by MT-ND3-linked, oxidative phosphorylation-dominant (OXPHOS-dominant) immune-metabolic features that was associated with subsequent poor seroconversion. The robustness of this signal was supported by donor-level sensitivity analyses, independent vaccine response cohorts, and cross-condition projection across immunocompromised settings. This program was characterized by poor alignment between metabolic activation, antigen presentation features, and immune activation programs, together with an inferred communication milieu less supportive of productive monocyte-T cell interaction. Regulatory modeling further nominated FOXO1 as a candidate coordinator of NR monocyte state progression. Together, these findings suggest that vaccine non-responsiveness may begin before immunization, as a measurable innate immune state that could help guide future risk stratification and intervention studies in high-risk hosts.

papers.title: Network toxicology and single-cell transcriptomics identify acrylamide- and glycidamide-related candidate biomarkers in diabetic ulcers.
papers.authors: Jiang Y, Tan Z, Cai Y, Hong S, Su Y, Ru Y, Li B.
papers.abstract: Diabetic ulcers (DU) are severe complications of diabetes, and environmental contaminants such as acrylamide (AA) and its metabolite glycidamide (GA) have been associated with metabolic disturbances relevant to diabetes. In this study, public transcriptomic datasets, network toxicology, protein interaction analysis, and machine learning were integrated to identify plausible candidate DU-associated biomarkers overlapping with predicted AA or GA targets. Functional enrichment, immune infiltration analysis, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and single-cell RNA sequencing were further applied to characterize their biological roles and cellular distribution. Eight candidate genes were identified from the intersection of differentially expressed genes and predicted toxicant targets, and PNP and CTSB were ultimately identified as plausible candidate DU-associated biomarkers. These genes were associated with proteasome function, DNA damage and repair, immune dysregulation, and altered cell communication. Single-cell analysis highlighted macrophages and T cells as major cell populations with dynamic plausible candidate biomarker expression. ELISA in streptozotocin induced diabetic ulcer mice further confirmed significantly increased CTSB and PNP protein levels, providing preliminary protein-level support for their association with DU. However, the overlap of PNP and CTSB with predicted AA/GA targets represents hypothesis-generating computational evidence only and does not establish that AA/GA exposure modulates these genes in vivo. These findings support PNP and CTSB as plausible candidate DU-associated biomarkers, while the predicted AA/GA-related associations require direct exposure-based experimental validation.

papers.title: Interleukin-10 in Endometriosis: Mechanistic Insights into Macrophage Plasticity, Immune Tolerance, and Lesion Persistence.
papers.authors: Hakimi M, Rezaee A, Rezaee N.
papers.abstract: Endometriosis is a chronic inflammatory yet immune-permissive disease in which ectopic endometrial-like lesions persist despite immune activation within the peritoneal cavity. Interleukin-10 (IL-10), traditionally regarded as an anti-inflammatory cytokine, has emerged as a context-dependent regulator of this paradox. This review critically synthesizes mechanistic evidence on IL-10 in endometriosis, with emphasis on macrophage polarization, immune tolerance, angiogenesis, stromal invasion, fibrosis, and lesion persistence. Current data do not support IL-10 as a uniformly elevated systemic biomarker. Instead, circulating IL-10 is inconsistent, whereas peritoneal-fluid and lesion-level IL-10 more closely reflect local immune organization. Macrophage involvement cannot be resolved by a simple M1/M2 axis. Single-cell, high-dimensional, and spatial studies instead identify lesion- and compartment-specific states that combine variable antigen presentation, phagocytosis, metabolic programming, stromal crosstalk, and repair-associated functions. Studies of plasmacytoid dendritic cell (pDC)-derived IL-10 provide mechanistic preclinical evidence for early angiogenic lesion establishment through IL-10R signaling and partly VEGF-dependent endothelial activation. Regulatory T cells (Tregs), IL-10-producing Th17 cells, NK-cell dysfunction, mast cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), and stromal cells further contribute to localized IL-10-associated networks that support immune escape and lesion adaptation. Importantly, IL-10 can become profibrotic in deep endometriosis by activating persistent STAT3-dependent myofibroblast and collagen programs in disease-conditioned stromal cells. Preclinical evidence does not support indiscriminate systemic IL-10 blockade or supplementation. Candidate strategies warranting further experimental investigation include local or upstream modulation of IL-10-producing niches, including pDC/CD36 signaling, Treg recruitment, macrophage chemokine and metabolic pathways, IDO1/IL-33 signaling, and fibrosis-associated IL-6/STAT3 contexts. In conclusion, IL-10 should be interpreted as a cellular-source-, compartment-, stage-, and lesion-state-dependent regulator of endometriosis persistence.

papers.title: Mapping the human intestinal immune landscape: Spatial profiling of dendritic cells, macrophages and T cells.
papers.authors: Gamero-Estevez E, Nattramilarasu PK, Müllertz O, Savochkina E, El Andalousi J, Hoebe K, Rückle T, Kim K, Dudziak D.
papers.abstract: Understanding how mucosal immunity is organized across the human intestine is essential for distinguishing responses to commensal from pathogenic bacteria. Using high-plex spatial proteomics and custom normalization algorithms, we mapped 6 million intestinal immune cells with a focus on T-cells, macrophages and dendritic cells (DC) across duodenum, jejunum, ileum, and descending colon in healthy human donors at single-cell resolution. Our pipeline enabled robust quantification of abundance and precise tissue-layer localization of immune cells across regions. We observed that memory CD103 + and cytotoxic CD8 + T cells comprise most of the intraepithelial lymphocytes; whereas effector CD4 + T cells are mostly present in the lamina propria. We also identified that CD163 + macrophages and CD1c + DC2, but not DC3, displayed a tissue dependent and heterogeneous expression profile of characteristic surface markers especially within the small intestine, but not colon environment. The precise tissue layer analysis further showed that DC3 were rare and restricted to the small intestinal submucosa, and that the expression of CD207 was reduced on colon DC2. Besides, CD103 was identified as reliable, layer-specific markers that identify mainly mucosal immune cells, and FXIIIA as one that distinguish submucosal from epithelial macrophages. This spatial atlas provides a comprehensive reference of intestinal myeloid organization in healthy donors and creates a framework for interpreting mucosal immune alterations in disease and for guiding targeted therapies.

papers.title: Co-expression of NKG2A-HLA-E and TIGIT-CD155 immune checkpoints is associated with immune dysfunction and poor survival in gastric cancer.
papers.authors: Zhuang X, Huang Y, Deng G, Hong C, Wang F, Wei Y, Feng W, Li Y, Tang Y, Lin Y, Chen S, Zhong S, Guo J, Yang Z, Zhang C, Deng C, He Y, Zhou G.
papers.abstract: The clinical significance of the NKG2A-HLA-E and TIGIT-CD155 immune checkpoint pathways in gastric cancer (GC) remains incompletely understood. We investigated their prognostic relevance and therapeutic potential using public datasets, a cohort of 195 patients, flow cytometry, single-cell RNA sequencing, multiplex immunofluorescence, and functional assays, with particular emphasis on cellular co-expression, spatial organization, and functional immune responses. HLA-E and CD155 expression was elevated in later-stage tumors, and concurrent high expression was associated with shorter overall and disease-free survival. Multivariable Cox regression identified the tumor-to-adjacent-normal HLA-E expression ratio as an independent prognostic factor. Flow cytometry linked NKG2A and TIGIT expression to distinct functional states of CD8⁺ T cells and NK cells from primary tumors and malignant ascites. Single-cell analyses revealed NKG2A and TIGIT co-expression in exhausted CD8⁺ T cell and CD56 bright NK cell subsets, together with HLA-E and CD155 co-expression in tumor epithelial cells. CellPhoneDB analyses predicted potential ligand-receptor interactions between tumor cells and infiltrating lymphocytes. Multiplex immunofluorescence demonstrated HLA-E and CD155 co-expression in tumor cells and close spatial proximity between HLA-E⁺ tumor cells and NKG2A⁺ lymphocytes. In ex vivo assays, combining NKG2A blockade with TIGIT or PD-1 blockade enhanced lymphocyte anti-tumor responses and organoid killing, with additional benefits over selected monotherapies. HLA-E or CD155 knockdown also enhanced immune cell function without further benefit from corresponding receptor blockade. Together, these findings suggest complementary immunoregulatory pathways associated with immune dysfunction and poor survival in GC, warranting independent prognostic validation and further preclinical evaluation of combination checkpoint blockade.

papers.title: CRC tumor antigens and immune escape: Designing peptide vaccines for colorectal Cancer.
papers.authors: Abbaszadeh S, Bahramibanan F, Naghavi Z, Heidari F, Alizadeh N, Soleimani M.
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a leading cause of global cancer mortality, with current therapies often limited by toxicity and resistance. Immunotherapy, particularly peptide-based vaccines, represents a promising alternative by eliciting targeted immune responses. This review provides a critical and comparative synthesis of CRC peptide vaccine development, distinguishing itself from previous reviews by integrating mechanistic insights into immune evasion with a structured framework that connects antigen selection, epitope identification (experimental and computational), and clinical translation. We specifically highlight two underexplored areas: tumor-associated neutrophils (TANs) and the critical distinction between microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) and microsatellite stable (MSS) CRC, which fundamentally dictates mutational burden, neoantigen load, and vaccine responsiveness. We first detail the sophisticated mechanisms of immune evasion employed by CRC, including an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment enriched with regulatory T cells (Tregs) and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), tumor-associated neutrophils (TANs), dysregulated antigen presentation via HLA class I alterations, and expression of inhibitory checkpoints. The review critically evaluates methods for epitope identification, contrasting traditional experimental approaches with modern computational strategies that leverage genomics, AI, and immunoinformatics tools for predicting high-affinity, immunogenic epitopes. We emphasize that predicted immunogenicity does not equate to clinical efficacy, and we critically appraise the limitations of current computational tools, including high false-positive rates and poor correlation with in vivo immunogenicity. While promising, challenges remain, including low immunogenicity, human leukocyte antigen (HLA) restriction, and tumor heterogeneity. Future success likely depends on developing multi-epitope, personalized vaccines combined with adjuvants and immune checkpoint inhibitors to enhance efficacy. In conclusion, peptide vaccines offer a precise and adaptable platform for CRC immunotherapy, holding significant potential for improving clinical outcomes through targeted immune activation.

papers.title: An Exploratory Simulation, Classification and Machine-Learning Workflow for Choosing an Antibody-Drug Conjugates (ADC) Conjugation-Platform.
papers.authors: Montefusco-Pereira CV.
papers.abstract: Choosing an ADC conjugation platform is an important early CMC decision because it affects drug-to-antibody ratio (DAR), product heterogeneity, stability, manufacturability, and development risk. However, this decision is still largely expert-driven, and few computational tools focus specifically on conjugation-platform selection. An reproducible Python workflow was developed to explore whether developability-related features could support ADC conjugation-platform classification. A balanced synthetic dataset of 48 records was generated across six platform archetypes. Models were trained and compared using Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting. Performance was assessed with hold-out testing, repeated and nested cross-validation, multiclass metrics, feature-ablation analysis, seed-sensitivity testing, and leave-one-named-platform-out analysis. Feature importance was examined and a Gradio interface was built as a demonstration tool. Random Forest achieved perfect accuracy in one 10-record hold-out split, but broader testing gave more cautious estimates, with repeated cross-validation accuracy of approximately 0.83 and macro F1 of approximately 0.81. Leave-one named-platform-out testing showed weaker transfer between platform families. Removing redundant features did not materially change internal performance. A literature-derived assessment of 20 ADC programs gave 4/20 agreement using a strict two-feature check and 16/20 agreement using a partly harmonized five-feature check; these analyses were interpreted as stress tests rather than external validation. This work provides a reproducible proof-of-concept workflow for ADC conjugation-platform modelling. Its current role is post-characterization classification and early process-optimization decision support after preliminary conjugation and analytical characterization, not pre-conjugation platform selection. Prospective experimental datasets and external validation are required before practical use.

papers.title: An Interpretable Machine Learning Model to Predict Skip Lymph Node Metastasis in Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma.
papers.authors: Jiang Z, Qiu M, Xie Y, Zhong X, Sheng H, Tang S, Zhang R, Qu X, Wan H, Zhai L, Huang D.
papers.abstract: Background Skip lymph node metastasis (SLNM) poses major diagnostic challenges for papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC), and existing prediction models rely merely on clinicopathological data and have limited predictive efficacy. This research constructed an interpretable machine learning prediction model integrating clinicopathological features and peripheral blood immune-inflammatory markers, aiming to realize personalized SLNM risk assessment and guide clinical treatment decision-making for patients with PTC. Methods Retrospective data from 1004 patients with PTC from the Second Affiliated Hospital of Nanchang were collected. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression filtered predictive variables, and seven supervised machine learning models were built to predict SLNM. Model discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility were evaluated via area under the curve (AUC), decision-curve analysis, and multiple auxiliary metrics, and the optimal algorithm was screened out. SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis interpreted feature contribution. Results Among all 1004 enrolled subjects, 193 (19.2%) presented with SLNM. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator analysis retained two immune-inflammatory markers-platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio and systemic immune-inflammation index-alongside five ultrasound-based clinical predictors: age, maximum tumor diameter, lesion site, multifocality and extrathyroidal extension. Extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) outperformed all other tested algorithms, with an AUC of 0.970 in the training cohort and an AUC of 0.897 in the internal validation cohort. SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis further assigned quantified importance weights to each predictor variable. Conclusions This study first integrated systemic immune-inflammatory biomarkers and clinicopathological indicators into an interpretable machine learning system then developed an open-access online prediction calculator. The model significantly improves SLNM predictive accuracy, providing quantitative evidence for individualized risk stratification and therapeutic management of PTC.

papers.title: A pseudo-ischemic tumor ecosystem couples malignant stress and inflammatory myeloid remodeling across adenocarcinomas.
papers.authors: Lu H, Abudukeremu D, Qi X, Zou M.
papers.abstract: Background Cancer-associated thrombosis and tumor immune remodeling may converge through hypoxia, myeloid inflammation, neutrophil extracellular traps, platelet engagement, and endothelial dysfunction. We investigated whether they define a conserved, transcriptomically measurable tumor state. Methods We integrated a lung adenocarcinoma extracellular-vesicle RNA dataset with three venous thromboembolism cohorts to derive five immunothrombotic modules. Single-cell RNA-sequencing data from lung (LUAD), pancreatic (PAAD), and gastric adenocarcinoma (STAD) were analyzed. We defined the pseudo-ischemic tumor ecosystem (PTES) as a transcriptomically defined molecular state reflecting coordinated malignant-cell stress and inflammatory-myeloid activity, rather than direct evidence of tissue ischemia or a diagnosis of cancer-associated thrombosis or venous thromboembolism. A tissue-resolved Core PTES, calculated as the mean of standardized malignant-stress and inflammatory-myeloid programs, was evaluated in 37 single-cell samples and 1107 TCGA tumors. Associations with immune states, Hallmark pathways, inferred cell-cell communication, and overall survival were assessed. The primary survival analysis used continuous Core PTES per one-standard-deviation increase, with high-versus-low PTES analyzed as a sensitivity analysis. Results Direct analysis showed the strongest effects for malignant stress (Hedges' g = 1.116), NET-like activity (g = 1.477), and endothelial activation (g = 1.288). Single-cell analysis retained 143,101 cells and localized malignant-stress and inflammatory-myeloid programs to their respective compartments. In TCGA, high Core PTES most strongly separated the inflammatory program (median difference = 1.134; rank-biserial r = 0.735). Cross-cancer GSEA identified recurrent proliferative, inflammatory, metabolic, and hypoxic programs, including E2F targets, G2M checkpoint, TNF-NF-κB, IL6-JAK-STAT3, glycolysis, and hypoxia. Inferred SPP1-CD44 and SPP1-ITGAV/ITGB1 interactions were detected across all three cancers. In multivariable models adjusted for age, sex, and stage, each one-standard-deviation increase in Core PTES was associated with poorer overall survival in LUAD (HR = 1.205, 95% CI 1.045-1.389) and PAAD (HR = 1.458, 95% CI 1.138-1.868), but not STAD (HR = 0.912, 95% CI 0.755-1.103); the cancer-stratified pooled HR was 1.168 (95% CI 1.060-1.288). High-versus-low sensitivity analyses showed the same cancer-specific pattern. Conclusion PTES captures a conserved pseudo-ischemic ecosystem linking malignant stress with inflammatory-myeloid remodeling. It is a hypothesis-generating, transcriptomically defined ecosystem measure rather than evidence of literal tissue ischemia, a diagnostic measure of cancer-associated thrombosis or venous thromboembolism, or a validated prognostic biomarker. Prospective clinical phenotyping and functional validation are required.

papers.title: ERV and trophoblast gene expression in retained products of conception.
papers.authors: Matsumoto R, Ota K, Takahashi T, Watanabe K, Saito W, Shimoya K, Nishimura H, Shiomi T, Kwak-Kim J, Mizukami Y, Mimura K.
papers.abstract: Retained products of conception (RPOC) may persist as focal, polypoid intrauterine lesions, but their molecular characteristics remain poorly defined. We performed the first transcriptome-wide comparison of hysteroscopically targeted RPOC and endometrial polyps, which may enter the same clinical and hysteroscopic differential diagnosis and served as pragmatic intrauterine comparators rather than tissue-matched controls (n = 6 per group). Bulk RNA sequencing was followed by pathway and molecular network analyses, and immune-receptor repertoires were reconstructed exploratorily. Relative to polyps, RPOC showed higher expression of trophoblast- and placental-function genes, including CSH1, CSH2, HSD3B1, CGA, HTRA4, PAPPA2, and GCM1, together with the endogenous retrovirus-derived genes ERVW-1 and ERVH48-1. Inflammation- and tissue-remodeling-associated genes, including MMP12, S100A8, S100A9, IL1B, IL6, and CXCL13, were also more highly expressed. Two KRAB-ZNF/KAP-associated transcriptional repression networks comprising 56 genes showed coordinated lower expression in RPOC. No individual transcript reached a false discovery rate-adjusted q value < 0.05 (minimum q = 0.095), and immune-repertoire analysis showed no reproducible group-specific pattern. Despite overlapping clinical and hysteroscopic appearances, the two lesions showed distinct exploratory gene-expression profiles. RPOC collected 51-134 days after the end of pregnancy or initial uterine treatment retained trophoblast-associated, ERV-associated, and inflammatory tissue-remodeling transcription, indicating that retained lesions are not necessarily biologically inert. These descriptive findings do not establish causality, direct KRAB-ZNF regulation of ERV loci, or predictive value for spontaneous resolution or intervention, but provide an initial molecular characterization of clinically retained RPOC and a basis for future longitudinal studies.

papers.title: Identification and Prioritization of Stage-Specific and Pan-Stage Therapeutic Targets in Hepatocellular Carcinoma Through Integrative Bioinformatics and Machine Learning Approaches.
papers.authors: Gudivada IP, Amajala KC, Kotha D.
papers.abstract: Introduction/objective Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) develops through a multistep process involving progressive molecular alterations from chronic liver disease to malignant transformation. Genes that change consistently across this progression, together with those unique to HCC, may offer insight into hepatocarcinogenesis and serve as candidate diagnostic and therapeutic targets. This study aimed to identify and prioritize stage-specific and pan-stage genes associated with HCC progression using an integrated bioinformatics and machine learning approach, and to evaluate their biological and diagnostic relevance. Methods The GEO dataset GSE89377, comprising 107 human liver tissue samples representing normal liver, hepatitis, cirrhosis, low- and high-grade dysplastic nodules, early HCC, and advanced HCC, was analyzed. Differentially expressed genes were identified using GEO2R, followed by protein-protein interaction network analysis using STRING and hub gene prioritization using Cytoscape/CytoHubba. In parallel, patient samples were classified into malignant and non-malignant groups using Random Forest (RF) and Support Vector Machine (SVM) models. Feature selection was performed within the training folds, and model performance was assessed using 5-fold nested stratified cross-validation, ROC/AUC analysis, and SHAP-based feature interpretation. Genes common to the bioinformatics and machine learning analyses were identified using the E-Venn tool to obtain stage-specific and pan-stage genes. The pan-stage genes were further evaluated using UALCAN, GTEx, and GEPIA, followed by Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA), LASSO regression, diagnostic nomogram construction and validation, and TIMER2.0-based immune-cell infiltration analysis. Results Bioinformatics analysis identified 100, 146, 220, 213, 181, and 209 differentially expressed genes in hepatitis, cirrhosis, low-grade dysplasia, high-grade dysplasia, early HCC, and advanced HCC, respectively. Machine learning analysis showed good discrimination between malignant and non-malignant samples, with RF and SVM achieving accuracies of 92.38% and 95.24%, respectively. SHAP analysis identified genes that contribute to the model's predictions, including TOP2A, KIF20A, PTTG1, and ZIC2. Integration of bioinformatics and machine learning analyses identified 14, 13, 13, 11, 12, and 19 stage-specific genes, respectively, and 10 pan-stage genes: ASPM, AURKB, CCNA2, CCNB2, CDKN3, HMMR, KIF20A, NUSAP1, PTTG1, and TOP2A. GSEA revealed predominant enrichment of cell-cycle and mitotic processes, particularly the G2/M checkpoint and E2F target pathways. LASSO regression prioritized PTTG1, HMMR, and KIF20A, which were used to construct a diagnostic nomogram with an AUC of 0.960 and a bootstrap-corrected AUC of 0.950. The model showed a sensitivity of 92.5% and specificity of 91.0%. These three genes also showed significant positive associations with immune cell infiltration in TCGA-LIHC, particularly with B cells, dendritic cells, and macrophages. Discussion The identified pan-stage genes were predominantly associated with cell-cycle regulation and proliferation-related biological processes, as supported by GSEA. The prioritization of PTTG1, HMMR, and KIF20A highlights their potential diagnostic relevance in HCC. Their associations with immune-cell infiltration further suggest possible links between these genes and the tumour immune microenvironment. Conclusion The integrated bioinformatics and machine learning analysis identified stage-specific and pan-stage genes associated with HCC progression. The 10 pan-stage genes were mainly associated with cell-cycle and proliferation-related processes. PTTG1, HMMR, and KIF20A were further prioritized as potential diagnostic biomarkers, with PTTG1 showing the major contribution to the diagnostic model. These findings provide candidate genes for further investigation in HCC; however, independent clinical and experimental validation is required.

papers.title: The KL and TLE1 anoikis-related signature predicts the diagnosis and indicates immune characteristics in endometriosis.
papers.authors: Wang J, Huang L, Huang H, Huang X, Huang L, Huang H, Huang F, Dong M, Wei B.
papers.abstract: Introduction Endometriosis (EMs) lacks non-invasive diagnostic biomarkers. Anoikis resistance enables ectopic endometrial cell survival, but key anoikis-related genes (ARGs) remain unclear. We aimed to identify a robust ARG-based diagnostic signature for EMs and explore its immune associations. Methods Four transcriptomic datasets (GSE7307 training; GSE7305, GSE23339, GSE51981 validation) were analyzed. DE-ARGs were identified by overlapping DEGs with 434 ARGs from GeneCards. Three machine learning algorithms (LASSO, random forest, SVM-RFE) screened core genes. ROC analysis evaluated diagnostic performance. A two-gene logistic regression model combining KL and TLE1 was also constructed, and its ROC performance was evaluated across training and validation cohorts. CIBERSORT and ssGSEA assessed immune infiltration. Single-cell RNA-seq (GSE179640) defined cell-type expression. qPCR and Western blotting validated expression in a small independent clinical cohort (n = 3 per group). Results 196 DE-ARGs were identified, significantly enriched in PI3K-AKT and focal adhesion pathways. KL and TLE1 were selected as core genes by all three algorithms. Both were consistently downregulated in EMs tissues across all cohorts (training AUC: KL=0.952, TLE1 =0.973; validation sets up to 1.000), substantially outperforming CA-125. The combined KL/TLE1 logistic model achieved AUCs of 1.000 in GSE7307, 1.000 in GSE7305, 1.000 in GSE23339, and 0.817 in GSE51981. Immune profiling revealed an immunosuppressive microenvironment with increased M2 macrophages and decreased NK cells, which correlated with KL/TLE1 downregulation. These findings indicate an association rather than a proven causal relationship. Single-cell analysis localized TLE1 to epithelial cells and KL to endothelial and fibroblast subsets. qPCR and Western blotting confirmed significant downregulation at both mRNA and protein levels. Discussion The KL/TLE1 signature exhibits excellent diagnostic accuracy for endometriosis in tissue-based analyses. This signature holds promise as a tissue-based diagnostic tool, but clinical translation will require larger prospective cohorts and validation in non-invasive samples such as menstrual effluent or circulating exosomes.

papers.title: Detoxification enzyme-related subtypes and prognostic stratification in cervical cancer: An integrated single-cell and transcriptomic analysis.
papers.authors: Li Y, Li H, Yang X, Gao Y, Wang X, Wei X.
papers.abstract: Background Cervical cancer (CC) is the second leading cause of cancer deaths in women globally. The prognostic relevance of transcriptional profiles associated with detoxification enzyme-related genes (DERGs) and their relationships with immune heterogeneity in cervical cancer (CC) remains unclear. Methods We obtained DERGs from GeneCards and analyzed TCGA-CESC data. Consensus clustering identified two DERG-associated subtypes, whose transcriptomic features were compared. A prognostic risk model was built using LASSO and Cox regression, then validated. Immune infiltration and scRNA-seq analysis were performed to investigate the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) of CC. The expression levels of prognostic genes were examined by RT-qPCR in clinical tissues and cell lines. Protein expression patterns were assessed using HPA database. Results The study identified two DERG-associated subtypes with significant survival differences, with Cluster 2 showing a more favorable prognosis. Subsequently, eight prognostic genes were identified based on differentially expressed genes between the two subtypes, and an eight-gene prognostic risk model was constructed (AUC > 0.8) in the TCGA-CESC cohort. High-risk group had lower immune cell infiltration and scores. A nomogram with risk score and N stage achieved AUC > 0.8 for survival prediction, while computational drug response analysis identified differences in predicted IC50 values for 13 agents between risk groups. The scRNA-seq analysis indicated a possible association between CH25H expression and macrophage states. The RT-qPCR results showed that, compared with the paired adjacent tissues, CD19, CD79B, C8G, CH25H and GNG8 were significantly down-regulated in the tumor tissues, while PCDHA11, PTGS2 and CYP26A1 were significantly up-regulated. Compared with H8 cells, the expressions of PTGS2 and CYP26A1 are higher in SiHa cells. Conclusions We identified DERG-associated molecular subtypes of CC and developed a prognostic model. Our findings may provide new insights into prognostic stratification and the TIME in CC.

papers.title: Integration of GWAS and Transcriptomic Data Links RMI1, ARHGEF15, TTC21B, and HAGH to Mitochondrial-Neuroinflammatory Coupling in Epilepsy.
papers.authors: Li K, Zhang H, Zhang J, Yang A.
papers.abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) identify epilepsy risk loci but often do not resolve the relevant regulatory genes, cell types, or disease-associated molecular programs. Subtype-resolved genetic evidence was integrated We therefore integrated subtype-resolved epilepsy GWASwith brain expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL), pathology-matched bulk transcriptomics, donor-aware single-cell data, and network analyses to prioritize susceptibility genes and metabolic-immune interaction axes. Summary statistics from eight epilepsy phenotypes underwent quality control, locus definition, SuSiE fine-mapping, brain eQTL colocalization, SMR-HEIDI analysis, and transcriptome-wide association testing. Genetically prioritized genes were evaluated in 162 bulk RNA-seq samples from four epilepsy pathologies and anatomically matched controls. Predefined metabolic and immune modules, cross-pathology coupling, CITE-seq localization in 85,780 cells from six donors, and donor-supported communication were integrated into a source-traceable network according to prespecified decision rules. Integration of 29 fine-mapped phenotype-locus records with colocalization, SMR-HEIDI, and transcriptome-wide association evidence prioritized four Tier 1 genes (RMI1, TVP23B, ARHGEF15, and TTC21B) and four Tier 2 genes (CDK5RAP3, GLS, SUGCT, and HAGH). Six colocalization records were strong, and eight were supportive. Seventeen of 32 gene-pathology results and 64 of 76 module-pathology results met prespecified criteria. Twenty metabolic-immune or gene-module edges and 11 communication interactions were accepted; the strongest coupling linked reduced oxidative phosphorylation with microglial activation (pooled ρ = -0.52) and IL1 signaling (ρ = -0.48). Five genes showed specific cellular localization. The primary network contained 18 nodes and 14 fully traceable edges; three additional relationships were retained only as supplementary contextual links. Convergent genetic, bulk transcriptomic, and single-cell evidence connected the prioritized susceptibility genes to mitochondrial function, glycolysis, lipid handling, neurotransmitter metabolism, microglial activation, cytokine signaling, and vascular or glial states. These findings define genetically anchored hypotheses and candidate pathways for experimental evaluation but do not establish causal direction, molecular interaction, or therapeutic efficacy.

papers.title: CCT2 is associated with autophagy-related changes and impaired anti-tumor function of CD8 + T cells in multiple myeloma.
papers.authors: Yan X, Zheng Y, Wang K, Jiang C, Lai B, Xu K, Chen Y, Shi C, Liu Y, Wang Z, Wu A, Wu H, Zhang P, Ouyang G.
papers.abstract: Multiple myeloma (MM) is a type of blood malignancy resulting from the uncontrolled proliferation of abnormal plasma cells in the bone marrow. Despite significant therapeutic advances over recent decades, MM remains high relapse rates and mortality, necessitating mechanistic insights to improve outcomes. Integrating an Affymetrix gene-expression microarray dataset and scRNA-seq from GEO, we evaluated the association between Chaperonin Containing TCP-1 Subunit 2 (CCT2) expression and autophagy activity in relapsed MM group. Autophagy-related gene modules were identified via autophagy scoring and weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), with subsequent functional annotation and pathway enrichment analysis of T cell subsets. Experimentally, CD8 + T cells from clinical samples were sorted for CCT2-knockdown models. CCT2 mRNA expression levels were quantified by qPCR, while cytotoxic capacity was assessed via ANNEXIN V-PI/FITC and LDH assays. ELISA measured cell activation level. Rescue experiments were performed by overexpressing CCT2 combined with Bafilomycin A1 (BafA1) treatment, with autophagy flux assessed by western blotting. Bioinformatics revealed CCT2 upregulation in relapsed MM group, strongly correlated with autophagy pathways and enriched in Naive/cytotoxic CD8 + T cell populations. In vitro experiments demonstrated that CCT2 knockdown enhanced CD8 + T cell cytotoxicity against MM cells, along with increased apoptosis, LDH release, and elevated IFN-γ/TNF-α/GZMB secretion. Conversely, CCT2 overexpression elevated autophagy and suppressed T cell cytotoxicity, which was partially reversed by autophagy inhibitors or ATG5 knockdown through restored cytokine production and cytotoxicity capacity. CCT2-related autophagy alterations are associated with reduced anti-tumor effector function of CD8 + T cells and may play a role in immune escape in MM. Our findings suggest that CCT2 is a potential therapeutic candidate target, and its role in regulating T cell function warrants further validation.

papers.title: Integrated bioinformatics analysis reveals matrix stiffness-related molecular signatures and mechanisms in osteoarthritis.
papers.authors: Gao F, Zhang X.
papers.abstract: Objective This study aimed to screen matrix stiffness-related diagnostic signature genes of osteoarthritis (OA) and clarify the underlying regulatory network, providing novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets for OA. Methods Two GEO transcriptomic datasets were integrated with matrix stiffness gene sets to obtain intersecting differentially expressed targets. WGCNA, PPI network and three machine learning algorithms (LASSO, SVM-RFE, Boruta) were applied to identify signature genes. ROC curves, nomogram and ssGSEA immune infiltration analysis were performed to assess diagnostic value and immune correlation. Clinical human cartilage samples and IL-1β-stimulated C28/I2 chondrocytes were used to verify ITGB5-related signaling via qRT-PCR, Western blot and cell functional assays. Results A total of five stiffness-associated OA signature genes including COL5A1, ITGB5, SPP1, FMOD, COL2A1 were identified with robust diagnostic efficiency. ITGB5 was correlated with cartilage sclerosis and positively correlated with pathogenic immune cells. Clinical tissue tests showed elevated ITGB5 and p-FAK as well as increased YAP nuclear translocation in OA cartilage. In vitro experiments confirmed that ITGB5 triggered chondrocyte matrix degradation and proliferative suppression through the downstream p-FAK/YAP cascade. Conclusion This study identified OA-related genes associated with matrix stiffness, and elaborated the ITGB5/p-FAK/YAP signaling axis, which linked cartilage remodeling and inflammatory immune microenvironment, offering promising clues for OA treatment.

papers.title: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic dissection of tumor-associated macrophage heterogeneity in cervical cancer: multi-omics perspectives and immunotherapy resistance.
papers.authors: Sayed U, Khdir MM, Jyothi S R, Maharana L, Gupta N, Singh D, Kadhim AM, Umarov D.
papers.abstract: Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) exhibit profound phenotypic and functional heterogeneity in cervical carcinoma, acting as key regulators of disease progression, extracellular matrix remodeling, and primary resistance to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB). This critical review synthesizes high-dimensional single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomics (ST) datasets to delineate distinct myeloid archetypes, principally osteoclast-like SPP1+ TAMs, phagocytic C1QC+ TAMs, and early-inflammatory CXCL9+ subsets. In high-risk human papillomavirus (hr-HPV)-driven tumors, viral oncoproteins E6 and E7 suppress cGAS-STING-dependent innate sensing and fuel CCL2 and CSF-1 chemokine secretion, driving stromal recruitment and preferential skewing toward immunosuppressive SPP1+ TAMs. Spatial transcriptomic profiling reveals that SPP1+ TAMs co-localize with alpha-SMA+ cancer-associated fibroblasts along invasive margins, forming dense desmoplastic mantles that physically and chemotactically exclude cytotoxic CD8+ T lymphocytes from tumor cores. Conversely, C1QC+ TAMs reside within coordinated peritumoral immune hubs that facilitate productive antigen presentation. We resolve critical evidence boundaries across multi-omics layers, establishing that while scRNA-seq and spatial mapping are rich in human cervical cancer, purified TAM epigenomics, proteomics, and direct metabolomics remain scarce, requiring cautious interpretation of cross-tumor extrapolations. Mechanistically, myeloid-mediated resistance is governed by a tripartite architecture: defective antigen recognition, spatial exclusion, and active effector exhaustion via PD-L1, TIM-3, and metabolic starvation. Finally, we evaluate therapeutic modalities, showing that pan-macrophage depletion via CSF1R inhibition carries off-target toxicities and rebound myeloid recruitment, whereas targeted functional reprogramming and spatial disruption offer superior translational potential.

papers.title: A deep-learning microglial response score integrates single-cell and spatial transcriptomics for Alzheimer's disease stratification.
papers.authors: Ren L, Ouyang W, Lai Z, Gong Z, Ling L.
papers.abstract: Background Microglia exhibit diverse responses in Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet linking these responses to tissue pathology and disease heterogeneity remains challenging. We aimed to develop a deep-learning microglial response score (DL-MRS) integrating single-cell, spatial and bulk transcriptomics to characterize AD-associated transcriptional patterns. Methods We analyzed human single-cell, spatial and bulk transcriptomic data to characterize microglial clearance and inflammatory programs. These programs and tissue-context features formed eight module-level inputs to a multilayer perceptron that generated DL-MRS. Model performance and feature contributions were assessed using five repeats of five-fold cross-validation, cross-cohort testing, feature-set comparisons and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis. Spatial localization, individual-level prediction using spatial transcriptomic data, and molecular heterogeneity within AD were also examined. Results Single-cell analyses characterized clearance-enriched and inflammation-enriched microglial groups. Descriptive spatial projection visualized regional variation in the weighted microglial and tissue-context programs. Across 697 AD and control bulk samples, DL-MRS achieved a repeated out-of-fold area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.939 and a mean cross-cohort transfer AUC of 0.947. SHAP analysis of the expanded model identified complement as the largest contributor, alongside contributions from microglial and tissue-context modules. Among 129 AD samples, median DL-MRS was higher in the immune-enriched than in the neuronal/synaptic-enriched molecular group (0.970 versus 0.800). These findings support DL-MRS as an interpretable research tool for integrating microglial and tissue-context signals to characterize AD-associated transcriptional patterns and within-disease molecular heterogeneity. Conclusion DL-MRS integrates microglial and tissue-context signals into an interpretable measure of AD-associated transcriptional remodeling. By capturing coordinated variation across immune, glial, vascular, neuronal and synaptic programs, DL-MRS reveals molecular heterogeneity among AD samples and provides a framework for investigating interindividual differences and advancing molecular stratification in AD research.

papers.title: Potential role of exercise-associated glucose metabolic reprogramming of immune cells in ameliorating chronic low-grade inflammation in type 2 diabetes mellitus: mechanisms and evidence.
papers.authors: Yang Q, Pang X, Peng X, Wang Z, Yang Y, Han Y.
papers.abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is often accompanied by chronic low-grade inflammation, an important driver of the development and progression of insulin resistance. The functional phenotypes of monocytes/macrophages and T cells involved in inflammatory responses are highly dependent on their intracellular glucose metabolic patterns. Immunometabolic research indicates that, in specific cell types and under particular activation conditions, some pro-inflammatory immune cells exhibit enhanced aerobic glycolysis, whereas some immune cells with anti-inflammatory or regulatory functions rely relatively more on mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. However, these metabolic-functional relationships are context-dependent and cannot serve as a universal basis for classifying all immune cells. This gives rise to an integrative hypothesis: beyond glucose-lowering and fat-loss effects, exercise may ameliorate chronic inflammation in T2DM by reshaping the functional profile of immune cells via reprogramming their glucose metabolic programmes. Whether such metabolic shifts serve as a direct mediator of the anti-inflammatory effects of exercise remains to be verified by metabolic flux measurements and mechanism-focused investigations. Centered on the cascade "exercise stimulation → altered immune-cell metabolic flux → remodelled inflammatory signalling → improved glycaemic control", this review summarises the features of disrupted glucose metabolism in immune cells and their proinflammatory mechanisms in T2DM. This review summarises the plausible molecular bases through which acute exercise and chronic training regulate immune cell metabolism via lactate signalling, the AMPK-mTOR-HIF-1α axis, epigenetic modifications and myokines. It distinguishes evidence obtained from human studies, animal experiments and in vitro cellular investigations, and discusses the effects of aerobic exercise, resistance training and high-intensity interval training, alongside limitations in head-to-head comparative evidence. Acute exercise triggers transient metabolic and signalling perturbations. Whether repeated bouts of exercise induce sustained immunometabolic adaptations through epigenetic regulation and mitochondrial remodelling constitutes the working model advanced herein; its stability and mediating role in patients with T2DM remain unconfirmed. We further perform an evidence-level appraisal of available data and identify critical gaps supporting this hypothesis, including the scarcity of direct metabolic flux measurements, limited accessibility of tissue-resident immune cell samples, and a lack of formal mediation analyses. Future work integrating stable-isotope tracing, single-cell multi-omics and mechanism-driven randomised controlled trials may help clarify whether glucose metabolic reprogramming mediates the anti-inflammatory effects of exercise. Such findings could lay a theoretical foundation for developing personalised exercise prescriptions for T2DM based on immunometabolic subtyping.

papers.title: The evolving immune ecosystem of TKI resistance in EGFR-mutant NSCLC: from treatment-induced remodeling to mechanism-guided therapy.
papers.authors: Luo B, Hairulajiang A, Liu J, Liu X.
papers.abstract: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have transformed the treatment of EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), yet acquired resistance remains a major clinical limitation. Resistance is increasingly understood as an evolving state shaped not only by tumor-cell genomic alterations but also by treatment-induced remodeling of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME). This Review examines how EGFR-TKI exposure reshapes macrophage states, T-cell function and localization, fibroblast and myeloid niches, and vascular architecture, and how these changes are reinforced by immune-checkpoint adaptation, metabolic reprogramming, and phenotypic plasticity. We then connect the evolving TIME to post-TKI therapeutic strategies according to the maturity of the supporting evidence, including immune checkpoint inhibitor-containing regimens, anti-angiogenic combinations, mechanism-matched targeted therapy, antibody-drug conjugates, bispecific T-cell engagers, and selected preclinical microenvironment-directed approaches. Finally, we discuss circulating biomarkers, single-cell sequencing, and spatial profiling as tools for longitudinally defining resistant immune states. Viewing TKI resistance as a temporally evolving immune ecosystem provides a framework for linking resistance mechanism, immune phenotype, and treatment selection rather than treating progression as a purely genomic endpoint.

papers.title: Proteomics and phosphoproteomics analysis of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma based on PD-L1 expression subtyping.
papers.authors: Chen Y, Gao B, Pan Y.
papers.abstract: Objective Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is a highly heterogeneous malignancy, and the clinical significance of PD-L1 expression has not yet been fully elucidated. This study aims to analyze the molecular differences between PD-L1-positive and PD-L1-negative DLBCL using omics approaches and to explore their potential regulatory mechanisms. Methods PD-L1 expression was assessed by immunohistochemistry in 72 cases of DLBCL and 12 cases of reactive hyperplasia (RH) lymph nodes as controls, followed by survival analysis. Three representative samples were selected from each of the PD-L1-positive DLBCL, PD-L1-negative DLBCL, and RH groups for data-independent acquisition (DIA) quantitative proteomics and phosphoproteomics analysis. Bioinformatics analyses included GO/KEGG enrichment analysis, PPI network construction, kinase-substrate enrichment analysis (KSEA), and motif analysis. Key findings were further validated in DLBCL cell lines via qRT-PCR and Western blotting, and functionally validated through CARD11 knockdown and PS-1145-mediated IKBKB inhibition. Results The PD-L1 positivity rate in DLBCL was 69.4%; PD-L1 positivity was significantly associated with poorer overall survival. Integrated proteomics and phosphoproteomics analyses revealed that, compared with PD-L1-negative DLBCL, CARD11 was the only protein in PD-L1-positive DLBCL that was upregulated at both the protein abundance and phosphorylation levels. KSEA and kinase-substrate network analyses predicted significant differences in IKBKB expression between PD-L1-positive and PD-L1-negative groups and identified CARD11 S515 as a potential downstream phosphorylation site of IKBKB. GSEA further indicated that the NF-κB signaling pathway was significantly enriched in Group A at both the protein and phosphorylation levels. In vitro validation confirmed that IKBKB, phosphorylated CARD11, phosphorylated P65, and PD-L1 were simultaneously upregulated in DLBCL cells; furthermore, knocking down CARD11 or inhibiting IKBKB reduced NF-κB pathway activity and PD-L1 expression. Conclusion These findings suggest that the IKBKB-CARD11-NF-κB-PD-L1 regulatory axis may be involved in immune evasion and poor prognosis in PD-L1-positive DLBCL. This regulatory axis provides omics evidence for PD-L1-based prognostic stratification and potential targeted combination immunotherapy strategies.

papers.title: Oxeiptosis-related transcriptional heterogeneity in lung adenocarcinoma: prognostic modeling and functional prioritization of PSMD2.
papers.authors: Cao Y, Chen F, Zhang H, Xia W, Li X, Zhang H, Xu Y.
papers.abstract: Background It remains uncertain whether transcriptional variation related to oxeiptosis carries prognostic information in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD). We investigated this question and sought a model-derived gene whose contribution could be examined experimentally. Methods Oxeiptosis-associated candidates were identified from TCGA-LUAD and used for tumor classification and survival modeling. Competing models were evaluated across six GEO cohorts, and gene contributions were examined by SHAP. We also analyzed immune-related expression and estimated drug IC 50 values with oncoPredict. The distribution of the model signature across cell populations was explored in GSE171145 using AUCell. PSMD2 was then silenced in A549 and PC9 cells, followed by qRT-PCR, wound-healing, and Transwell assays. Results The 45-gene panel separated TCGA-LUAD tumors into four expression groups, of which C3 contained greater immune and stromal components. Bidirectional stepwise Cox regression followed by ridge regression produced the best overall performance across the six evaluation cohorts (mean C-index, 0.669). The resulting model comprised PSMD2, LSG1, PTBP1, ELAVL1, ANP32B, IMMT, and HSPD1. After adjustment for age, sex, and pathological stage, each standard deviation increase in the risk score corresponded to a higher mortality risk (HR, 1.62; 95% CI, 1.41-1.85). Survival separation reached significance in TCGA and four GEO cohorts, whereas the remaining two datasets showed the same direction without statistical significance. The score tracked positively with cell-cycle and DNA-replication activity, while the high-risk group expressed lower levels of the examined HLA genes. Drug-response estimation associated lower risk with greater predicted sensitivity to ribociclib and higher risk with greater predicted sensitivity to BI-2536. At single-cell resolution, high AUCell scores occurred mainly in epithelial and myeloid populations. PSMD2 made the largest SHAP contribution, and its silencing impaired migration and invasion in both cell lines. Conclusion The seven-gene model links oxeiptosis-related expression to LUAD prognosis, immune features, and predicted drug sensitivity. The prognostic contribution of PSMD2 and the effects of its knockdown support further investigation of its function.
